title: 3 Mar 2024 (Pearson VUE, recall C)
des: DOH (HAAD) paediatrics recall, Pearson VUE exam 3 March 2024 (third recall, notes scanned 6 March 2024)

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia has recurrent infections. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Recurrent splenic infarction leaves children with SCD functionally asplenic, susceptible to encapsulated bacteria; give penicillin prophylaxis and vaccines.

questions.question: A child has fever, petechial rash and meningism. The slide shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the organism?
questions.exp: Gram-negative diplococci in CSF with a purpuric rash = meningococcus. Pneumococcus is Gram-positive diplococci.

questions.question: A child has meningococcal meningitis (slide shown). Which statement is correct?
questions.exp: MenC, MenACWY and MenB vaccines have greatly reduced cases. Dexamethasone benefit is shown mainly for Hib and pneumococcal meningitis (hearing loss).
questions.a: It is caused by a Gram-positive organism
questions.b: Cases have decreased after the vaccination programme
questions.c: Dexamethasone is proven effective in meningococcal meningitis

questions.question: A child has a boggy circular scalp lesion with pustules and pus (kerion). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Kerion is inflammatory tinea capitis (often Trichophyton tonsurans/Microsporum): systemic antifungal for 6–8 weeks; topical treatment alone fails.
questions.a: Oral griseofulvin (or terbinafine) after scalp scrapings

questions.question: A child has a circular scaly skin lesion with raised edges and central clearing. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Tinea corporis (ringworm) is treated with topical imidazole or terbinafine for 2–4 weeks; steroids worsen it (tinea incognito).

questions.question: Which statement about retinopathy of prematurity treatment is correct?
questions.exp: Laser ablation of avascular retina is for type 1 ROP; complications include exudative detachment, cataract and myopia. Stage 4–5 detachment needs vitreoretinal surgery.
questions.a: Laser is given only after detachment
questions.b: A demarcation line (stage 1) needs urgent laser
questions.c: Exudative retinal detachment is a recognised complication of laser therapy
questions.d: Stage 4 ROP can be fully treated with laser

questions.question: Which statement about long QT syndrome is correct?
questions.exp: Genetic testing identifies a mutation (KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A) in about 75–80% of clinically definite LQTS. Hypokalaemia (not hyperkalaemia) prolongs QT. Beta-blockers are first-line. The recall marked the hyperkalaemia option.
questions.c: About 75–80% of congenital cases have an identified genetic cause
questions.d: Hyperkalaemia commonly causes acquired long QT

questions.question: What is the preferred site for intraosseous access in a child?
questions.exp: Anteromedial proximal tibia, 1–3 cm below the tibial tuberosity.

questions.question: Which presentation most suggests non-accidental injury?
questions.exp: Bruising in a non-mobile infant ('those who don't cruise rarely bruise') is a red flag; a short fall rarely causes significant injury.
questions.b: A 3-month-old with bruises and a history of falling from the changing table
questions.c: A 10-year-old with a forearm fracture from a fall
questions.d: A toddler with a forehead bruise after a fall

questions.question: An infant has a rib fracture with no clear history. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Any unexplained fracture in an infant needs a full skeletal survey (repeated at 11–14 days), CT head under 1 year, and safeguarding.

questions.question: A known asthmatic has severe distress and cannot complete a sentence despite initial treatment. What is next?
questions.exp: Severe/life-threatening asthma not responding to bronchodilators and steroids: IV magnesium sulfate.

questions.question: A stable child has SVT on ECG. Vagal manoeuvres fail. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Adenosine by rapid bolus with flush; cardioversion only if unstable.

questions.question: An 8 kg infant with SVT is haemodynamically unstable. What do you do?
questions.exp: Unstable SVT: synchronised cardioversion 1 J/kg, increasing to 2 J/kg. Unsynchronised defibrillation (4 J/kg) is for VF/pulseless VT.
questions.a: Synchronised DC shock 8 J (1 J/kg), then 16 J (2 J/kg)

questions.question: An ECG shows Wolff–Parkinson–White pattern. Which association is recognised?
questions.exp: Ebstein anomaly has accessory pathways (WPW) in 10–25%; also associated with congenitally corrected TGA and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

questions.question: A mother with SLE has a baby born with complete heart block. Which statement is correct?
questions.exp: Congenital heart block from maternal anti-Ro/La damages the conducting system permanently; most affected babies need a pacemaker (about two-thirds) in childhood. The recall marked 'pacemaker whatever the cause'.
questions.a: Many will need a pacemaker, and the block is permanent
questions.b: It resolves once maternal antibodies clear
questions.d: Only 20% will ever need a pacemaker

questions.question: An intubated child has poor chest rise and unequal air entry. What do you do first?
questions.exp: DOPES: Displacement (right main bronchus intubation gives unequal entry), Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment, Stomach. Check tube depth and pull back if too deep.
questions.c: Reposition (pull back) the endotracheal tube after checking its position

questions.question: After an RTA a child has BP 70/40 and needs sedation for intubation. Which drug is preferred?
questions.exp: Ketamine maintains blood pressure (sympathomimetic) and is preferred in haemodynamically unstable patients.

questions.question: Four hours after pancreatectomy a child has severe pain and low blood pressure. What do you do first?
questions.exp: Post-operative hypotension is bleeding or third-space loss until proved otherwise: resuscitate with fluid (and blood) while getting surgical review.
questions.b: IV fluid bolus 10–20 mL/kg and call the surgeon

questions.question: In PICU 4 hours after resuscitation and intubation, a child has normal BP but capillary refill of 3–4 seconds and cold hands. What do you do?
questions.exp: Prolonged capillary refill with cold peripheries indicates compensated shock; give 10 mL/kg fluid and reassess before inotropes.

questions.question: A child is in cardiogenic shock. Which drug is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Cardiogenic shock needs inotropy with afterload reduction (dobutamine, milrinone); adrenaline if hypotensive. Avoid large fluid boluses.

questions.question: A child in shock in ICU has received two 20 mL/kg saline boluses and remains shocked. What is next?
questions.exp: Fluid-refractory septic shock: start adrenaline (cold) or noradrenaline (warm) infusion, peripherally if needed.

questions.question: A child had hives on first eating egg and is due for influenza vaccination. What do you do?
questions.exp: Egg allergy, even anaphylaxis, is not a contraindication to influenza vaccine (ovalbumin content is very low); give in a normal setting (JCVI/AAP).
questions.a: Give a split dose under observation
questions.b: Refer to an allergist for testing first

questions.question: When should a preterm neonate receive the hexavalent (6-in-1) vaccine?
questions.exp: Preterm babies are vaccinated by chronological age without correction; very preterm infants get the first doses in hospital with apnoea monitoring.
questions.a: At 2 months chronological age, as for term babies

questions.question: A preterm baby with RDS was put on CPAP at 4 hours of age; at 10 days he still needs nasal oxygen. What would most likely have prevented prolonged respiratory problems?
questions.exp: Early CPAP from birth with selective surfactant (LISA) reduces BPD compared with ventilation. Antenatal steroids are the strongest preventive measure.
questions.a: CPAP from the first minutes of life with early surfactant as needed

questions.question: A 14-year-old has weight loss, exercises 2–3 hours a day, and has dental erosion and calluses on the knuckles. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Russell sign (knuckle calluses) and dental erosion indicate self-induced vomiting. With significant weight loss this can be anorexia binge-purge type; the recall keyed anorexia.

questions.question: A doctor compares patients admitted who received a certain IV fluid with patients who did not, using hospital records at one point in time. What type of study is this?
questions.exp: The recall keyed cross-sectional (no random allocation, exposure and outcome at the same time). If patients are followed forward, it becomes a cohort study.

questions.question: A mother with a family history of breast cancer wants her 14-year-old daughter screened (BRCA). Which ethical principle supports waiting?
questions.exp: Predictive testing for adult-onset conditions is deferred until the young person can decide, respecting her future autonomy.

questions.question: Which electrolyte is known to fall during the early phase of refeeding in anorexia nervosa?
questions.exp: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome.

questions.question: A baby has rocker-bottom feet, small mouth, micrognathia and cleft palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, clenched fists with overlapping fingers and small mouth = Edwards. Patau has cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly and polydactyly. The recall marked trisomy 13 (cleft palate); both have rocker-bottom feet.

questions.question: A short boy has a congenital heart defect (pulmonary stenosis) and infertility. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Noonan (PTPN11): short stature, pulmonary valve stenosis, webbed neck, cryptorchidism and reduced fertility in males; normal karyotype.

questions.question: A girl has absent corpus callosum, infantile spasms and chorioretinal lacunae. What is the syndrome?
questions.exp: Aicardi syndrome (X-linked dominant, girls): agenesis of the corpus callosum, infantile spasms and chorioretinal lacunae.

questions.question: How is Prader–Willi syndrome confirmed?
questions.exp: Methylation analysis detects all three mechanisms (paternal deletion, maternal UPD, imprinting defect); FISH only finds deletions.
questions.b: DNA methylation study of chromosome 15q11–13 (FISH detects deletions)

questions.question: A child has painless rectal bleeding with maroon stools. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa causes painless bleeding in young children; the Meckel scan detects gastric mucosa.

questions.question: How is central precocious puberty diagnosed?
questions.exp: Confirm activation of the axis with basal/stimulated LH, then MRI brain (especially in boys and girls under 6). The recall marked cranial imaging.
questions.c: GnRH stimulation test (raised LH), then cranial MRI

questions.question: A boy has only sparse pubic hair at the base of the penis. What Tanner stage is this?
questions.exp: Pubic hair stage 2: sparse long lightly pigmented hair at the base of the penis.

questions.question: A child has recurrent infections without pus, and delayed separation of the umbilical cord. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: LAD type 1 (CD18): delayed cord separation (>3 weeks), omphalitis, very high neutrophil counts and infections without pus.

questions.question: A boy has recurrent bacterial infections, and on examination there is no lymphoid tissue and no tonsils. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: BTK mutation: absent B cells, very low immunoglobulins, absent tonsils and lymph nodes, infections after 6 months.

questions.question: A child with liver disease has a raised INR and PT and is bleeding. What is true about treatment?
questions.exp: Cholestasis causes vitamin K malabsorption, which corrects with IV vitamin K; synthetic failure does not, and needs FFP for bleeding.
questions.a: Vitamin K always corrects liver coagulopathy
questions.b: Vitamin K will improve the INR if it is due to deficiency; FFP if bleeding

questions.question: A boy known to have factor IX deficiency (haemophilia B) has profuse bleeding. What do you give?
questions.exp: Replace the missing factor promptly (recombinant factor IX); vitamin K does not correct haemophilia.

questions.question: A teenager was found unresponsive in the bathroom and died despite resuscitation. How should the family be told?
questions.exp: Breaking bad news: senior clinician involved, private room, clear language, allow questions and support.
questions.c: The doctor who led the resuscitation tells them in a private place what happened and the possible cause

questions.question: A 15-month-old has missed two vaccine appointments despite many calls; the mother finally brings him. What do you do?
questions.exp: Never miss an opportunity: give catch-up vaccines; there is no need to restart the schedule.
questions.a: Do not vaccinate; it is too late
questions.b: Only talk to the mother about vaccination

questions.question: An intubated preterm neonate has increasing abdominal size and vomits after each feed; X-ray is normal. What do you do?
questions.exp: Feed intolerance with a normal X-ray: monitor residuals and girth, consider reducing or pausing feeds, and watch for NEC.
questions.a: Check gastric residuals before each feed and monitor abdominal girth

questions.question: A ventilated neonate deteriorates with a pneumothorax. What is the risk factor?
questions.exp: Volutrauma and barotrauma cause air leak.

questions.question: A child with glycogen storage disease has glycogen deposits on muscle biopsy (Pompe disease). Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Pompe disease (GSD II): lysosomal acid α-1,4-glucosidase deficiency.

questions.question: A child has a typical picture of homocystinuria. How is it diagnosed?
questions.exp: Cystathionine β-synthase deficiency: high plasma homocysteine and methionine. Some respond to pyridoxine.
questions.c: Raised plasma total homocysteine (and urine homocystine)

questions.question: What advice do you give about exercise for a 5-year-old boy with Down syndrome?
questions.exp: Encourage activity; teach parents the signs of cervical cord compression (neck pain, gait change, weakness).
questions.a: He can do any sport freely without precautions
questions.c: Special Olympics require routine neck X-rays
questions.d: There is a risk of atlantoaxial instability; report symptoms of cord compression

questions.question: A child in status epilepticus has had two doses of rectal diazepam and is still seizing. What is next?
questions.exp: APLS: after two benzodiazepine doses give a second-line drug: phenytoin 20 mg/kg or levetiracetam 40 mg/kg; then RSI with thiopental.

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl has bilateral enlarged cervical lymph nodes. When should excision biopsy be considered?
questions.exp: Biopsy nodes that are growing, persist beyond 4–6 weeks, are over 2 cm, supraclavicular, or with systemic symptoms or mediastinal widening.
questions.a: If they have not reduced in size after 2 weeks
questions.c: If the nodes have not resolved after 4–6 weeks (or are growing)

questions.question: A girl has a unilateral posterior cervical lymph node, facial oedema and distended neck veins. What do you do?
questions.exp: Facial swelling and distended neck veins indicate SVC obstruction from a mediastinal mass (lymphoma): urgent CXR, careful anaesthesia and biopsy.
questions.a: Urgent work-up: chest X-ray and excision biopsy

questions.question: A 3-year-old with a URTI took paracetamol and ibuprofen. After 4 days he has itchy red circular lesions on the back; examination is otherwise normal. What do you do?
questions.exp: Post-viral urticaria is common and self-limiting; antihistamines help. NSAIDs can worsen urticaria, so avoiding ibuprofen is reasonable. The recall marked stopping both drugs.
questions.b: Give an antihistamine and reassure (acute urticaria / urticaria multiforme)

questions.question: A child with systemic JIA has macrophage activation syndrome. Which findings are typical?
questions.exp: MAS: persistent fever, hyperferritinaemia, cytopenias, raised liver enzymes and triglycerides, low fibrinogen (so ESR falls). Treat with steroids, ciclosporin or anakinra.
questions.c: Very high ferritin and raised transaminases with falling ESR and platelets

questions.question: Which factor increases the risk of coronary aneurysms in Kawasaki disease?
questions.exp: Prolonged fever, delayed IVIG, IVIG resistance, age under 1 or over 8 years, and male sex increase risk.
